title: Locate a bracket on one round pin and one diamond pin, flats facing the round pin
instruction: Locate the blue bracket on the fixture by its two holes: stand one round pin in one socket and the diamond pin in the other, turned so its two flat sides face the round pin, then lay the bracket flat on the fixture over both pins.
context: Machining, drilling, welding and inspection fixtures, and the nests and pallets of robot cells, locate a part by two of its holes with one round pin and one diamond (relieved) pin. The round pin fixes the part's position; the diamond pin, ground with two flats so that only two narrow lands remain, only stops the part turning. Its flats must face the round pin, so that the difference between the part's hole spacing and the fixture's pin spacing, which is never exactly zero, is taken up along the line between the holes. Two round pins, or a diamond pin turned a quarter turn, over-constrain the part: it jams or will not go down over both. Fitting the pins the right way is part of building or changing over a fixture, done by tool and die makers (O*NET 51-4111.00) and machinists (51-4041.00).
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Everything is square to the table's edges. Five kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Fixture plate: a dark grey steel plate 100 mm along x, 250 mm along y and 15 mm thick, fixed to the table, centred at x 30.0 cm, y 0. Two square sockets, 55 x 55 mm, go through it, centred at x 30.0 cm, y +5.0 cm (socket A, on the robot's left) and y -5.0 cm (socket B), 100 mm apart; the table is their floor. (2) Two round locating pins: bright steel cylinders 48 mm across and 55 mm tall, 100 g each (hollow; solid steel would weigh 780 g), standing upright on the right tray at x 22.0 cm, y -23.5 cm and x 22.0 cm, y -29.5 cm. A pin in a socket has 3.5 mm of play either side. (3) Diamond pin: one rigid part 55 mm tall, 80 g (hollow): a round bright steel shank 48 mm across and 15 mm tall with a black steel head on top, a bar 48 mm long, 8 mm wide and 40 mm tall centred on the shank. The bar's two 48 x 40 mm faces are the flats; its two 8 mm ends are the lands. It stands shank down on the left tray at x 23.5 cm, y +25.0 cm, the head's long side along y (along the line between the sockets). In a socket the shank fills the plate's thickness and the head stands above the plate. (4) Bracket: one rigid blue acetal part, 190 g: a plate 88 mm (x) by 212 mm (y) and 10 mm thick with two square through-holes, 64 x 64 mm, centred on its long centre line 62 mm either side of its middle (124 mm apart), and a block 30 mm (x) by 40 mm (y) and 25 mm tall fixed on top at its centre (the grip boss). It lies flat on the table, boss up, centred at x 13.5 cm, y +11.0 cm, its long side along y. (5) Two trays: black rubber mats 3 mm thick, fixed: on the left 90 x 90 mm centred at x 23.5 cm, y +25.0 cm; on the right 90 mm (x) by 150 mm (y) centred at x 22.0 cm, y -26.5 cm. Nothing else is on the table. Clearances: over a round pin a hole has 8 mm of clearance on every side; over the diamond with its flats facing the other socket, 28 mm along the line between the sockets and 8 mm across it. The holes are 24 mm farther apart than the sockets, so with a round pin in B and the diamond in A, flats facing B, the bracket goes down over both only with its centre 4 to 16 mm to the left of the fixture's centre (with the round pin in A and the diamond in B, 4 to 16 mm to the right), with the pins centred in their sockets; wherever they stand in their play, that range is at least 5 mm wide. Over two round pins, or over the diamond turned a quarter turn (48 mm along the line), it cannot come down over both (it misses by 8 mm with the pins centred, by at least 1 mm wherever they stand) and rests on the pin heads.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the poses of the three pins and the bracket (in a real trial: a photo from above, a ruler and a feeler gauge). A pin is fitted in a socket when it stands upright (its axis within 5 degrees of vertical; a round pin either end down, the diamond shank down), the centre of its bottom face is inside that socket's 55 x 55 mm opening seen from above and within 3 mm of the table (the socket's floor), and it is at rest (neither end of its axis moved more than 2 mm in the last 0.5 s). The diamond is turned right when, seen from above, the long side of its head is within 15 degrees of square to the line between the two sockets (its flats face the other socket). A located set is a round pin fitted in one socket and the diamond fitted in the other, turned right. The bracket is seated when it lies flat at the plate's height (boss up, level within 2 degrees, every corner of its underside within 2 mm of the plate's top), every fitted pin stands in one of its holes (the pin's axis passes through the bracket inside a hole's 64 x 64 mm outline, a different hole for each pin), and it is at rest (neither hole's centre moved more than 2 mm in the last 0.5 s). Score 0 if any pin or the bracket is off the table (its centre outside the table's outline seen from above, or its lowest point more than 10 mm below the table top), or if no pin is fitted. Otherwise: 0.25 if a pin is fitted but there is no located set (one pin only, two round pins, or the diamond not turned right; a bracket seated over such pins still scores 0.25); 0.5 for a located set with the bracket not seated (on the table, held up, resting on the pin heads, over one pin only, or still moving); 1.0 for a located set with the bracket seated over both pins. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. There is no 0.75: with a located set the bracket either comes down over both pins or it does not. Success: 1.0 held for 2.5 s. The scorer reads only the pins and the bracket, not the grippers, so a part held still in place is scored where it stands (holding the bracket cannot bring it down over a wrong set).
fidelity: Clearances are exaggerated several hundredfold so the over-constraint shows at robot accuracy: 48 mm pins in 64 mm holes and a hole spacing 24 mm longer than the pin spacing (real fits and errors are hundredths of a millimetre), standing for a part at its tolerance limit. The diamond's head is a flat-sided bar (real ones keep two narrow round lands). Pins stand loose in sockets with 3.5 mm of play, not pressed in, and are hollow. Rigid bodies, default friction.
reset_notes: Put the two round pins upright on the right tray at x 22.0 cm, y -23.5 cm and x 22.0 cm, y -29.5 cm; the diamond pin shank down on the left tray at x 23.5 cm, y +25.0 cm, its head's long side along y; the bracket flat, boss up, centred at x 13.5 cm, y +11.0 cm, its long side along y. Both sockets empty. Nothing is consumed.
